stage_description: Beyond about two years a mouse is very old, and few individuals reach two and a half to three years. This final stage brings marked frailty: significant loss of weight and muscle, a poor coat, reduced mobility, possible large tumours, and laboured breathing. Care now shifts from prevention to comfort, with ongoing assessment of the mouse's quality of life.
nutrition: Prioritise palatable, easy-to-eat food: soften pellets, offer nutrient-dense favourites, and hand-feed if needed to keep the mouse eating and drinking. Make sure food and water sit within very easy reach, and offer any small fresh treats the mouse still enjoys to support intake and hydration.
activity: Comfort now matters more than exercise. Provide low, easy access with extra-soft, warm bedding, and remove tall structures and unsafe wheels to prevent injury. Keep the environment warm, quiet, and stable, handle the mouse gently with minimal stress, and maintain companionship if the group remains peaceful.
veterinary_check_frequency: Work closely with your exotics or rodent-savvy veterinarian on comfort and quality-of-life assessment, with visits as needed rather than on a fixed schedule. Discuss palliative options honestly, and when suffering begins to outweigh comfort, talk through humane euthanasia together.
dental_care: Keep offering soft gnaw items and check the incisors often, because teeth overgrow quickly once a mouse stops gnawing. If overgrown teeth stop the mouse from eating, a veterinary trim restores comfort, and softening the food further eases feeding.
warning_signs: Contact your vet promptly about signs of pain or distress, laboured or open-mouthed breathing, refusal to eat or drink, inability to reach food or water, self-isolation, a large ulcerated tumour, or dehydration. These call for a discussion about comfort care and humane options.
disclaimer: This information is for educational purposes only and does not replace consultation with a veterinarian.
